documents: Chiu et al. 2022, Hydrological Processes 36:e14611, published paper (PDF, 11 pages)

entry.evidence: Hence, questions are still remained how seasonal changes in ET after timber harvesting in catchment scale.

steps.action: Frame the open question of how catchment-scale ET changes seasonally after timber harvesting. Annual water balance studies cannot resolve this, and single-year STWB applications give little information.
steps.quote: Hence, questions are still remained how seasonal changes in ET after timber harvesting in catchment scale.

steps.action: Propose that strip-thinning, by raising light availability and understory growth, may change the seasonal pattern of ET change.
steps.quote: seasonal patterns of changes in evapotranspiration after timber harvesting possibly differ

steps.action: Design the study as an STWB water-loss estimate applied to paired treated and control catchment runoff data. The STWB method is chosen over the annual water balance because storage changes matter at monthly scale.
steps.quote: we applied the STWB model for evaluating the effects of 50% strip-thinning on annual and seasonal evapotranspiration

steps.action: Set the conditions in the field: 50% strip-thinning of 10.9 ha in KT (July-December 2011, shrubs removed July 2011) while KC is kept unthinned. Pre-, during- and post-thinning periods are defined.
steps.quote: 50% strip-thinning operation was applied in the KT catchment (treatment catchment)

steps.action: Monitor discharge (V-notch weirs and Parshall flumes, 10-min loggers), climate (weather station, tipping-bucket gauge) and groundwater in two boreholes from July 2010 to December 2012. Missing discharge days are filled by an inter-catchment linear regression.
steps.quote: The discharge was measured at catchment outlets

steps.action: Compare precipitation, runoff coefficients, flow duration curves and event responses before and after thinning. Low flow is reduced in KT after thinning, but daily flow shows no significant pre/post difference by t-test.
steps.quote: significant runoff reduction during low flow period after thinning in catchment KT was observed

steps.action: Estimate daily, monthly and annual water loss (ET) in both catchments with the STWB model. Hydrological periods of 8-100 days are assumed to have equal storage at start and end.
steps.quote: The annual WLSTWB in the catchment KT was 840 mm/year during the pre-thinning period and 780 mm/year during the post-thinning period

steps.action: Tabulate annual water loss from the simple annual water balance (P-Q) alongside the STWB estimates for both catchments and periods. The two methods give different magnitudes (e.g., KT pre 980 vs 840 mm).
steps.quote: water loss calculated using the WB method (WLWB) and the STWB method (WLSTWB)

steps.action: Fit a pre-treatment calibration regression of monthly KT on KC water loss (beta1 = 0.84, r2 = 0.93). Predict KT post-thinning water loss without treatment and take the residuals as monthly treatment effects.
steps.quote: The calibration equation of water loss in the catchment KT and KC was significant

steps.action: Test post-thinning treatment effects against the residuals of the pre-thinning calibration by t-test. The result is not significant (p = 0.78).
steps.quote: showed no significant difference in the residuals of the calibration equation

steps.action: Read the seasonal sequence of monthly treatment effects: lower water loss from September 2011 to May 2012, higher from May to December 2012.
steps.quote: was constantly low compared to pre-thinning conditions

steps.action: Compare the STWB annual water-loss change in KT with the independent plot-scale ET measurements (interception, transpiration, floor evaporation) of Sun et al. (2017) inside KT. The direction is similar, but pre-thinning water loss is smaller here.
steps.quote: This result is similar to the finding by Sun et al. (2017)

steps.action: Use understory species counts and coverage from four monitoring plots, reported in Onda & Gomi (2021), showing understory increase after thinning.
steps.quote: The average understory vegetation coverage was slightly increased

steps.action: Propose regrowth of understory vegetation (interception and transpiration) as the explanation for the reduced treatment effect in the growing season.
steps.quote: interception and transpiration from the regrowth understory vegetation may partially explain the decrease in treatment effect in ET

steps.action: Match the summer-high, winter-low seasonality of water loss to published transpiration seasonality in Japanese cypress forests and to understory phenology.
steps.quote: Previous studies have reported the significant seasonality of transpiration in Japanese cypress forests

steps.action: Compare the annual treatment effect (about 20 mm/year) with cross-catchment syntheses (Bosch & Hewlett 1982; Stednick 1996) and find it much lower.
steps.quote: The annual treatment effect of water loss in our catchment was relatively low (approximately 20 mm/year) compared with that in previous studies.

steps.action: Report the change in water loss from both the paired-catchment method and the single-catchment method. They differ by a factor of three (20 vs 60 mm).
steps.quote: the changes in water loss were 20 and 60 mm when the paired and single catchment methods were applied

steps.action: List candidate factors for the small effect: precipitation, species, and increased forest-floor evaporation. None is tested.
steps.quote: suggesting that other factors, such as precipitation (Dung et al., 2012), species

steps.action: Support the precipitation and management-type factors with published results from other thinned catchments (Dung et al. 2012; Kubota et al. 2018; Lane & Mackay 2001; Hawthorne et al. 2013; Sahin & Hall 1996).
steps.quote: Precipitation affected water loss in the catchments with the same species and similar timber removal percentages.

steps.action: Keep the claim that ET decreased immediately after thinning through canopy removal and that treatment effects increased about 5 months later, attributed to understory recovery.
steps.quote: Treatment effects have decreased immediately after thinning, imply that ET decreased because of the removal of canopy trees.

tree.answer: Seasonal and annual change in catchment ET after 50% strip-thinning
No; ET is inferred from precipitation minus runoff via the STWB model
Estimate annual and monthly treatment effects on ET
Only post hoc candidate factors (understory regrowth, precipitation, species, floor evaporation)
No distinct predictions derived for the candidate factors
Set: thinning applied to KT with KC as unthinned control
Partly; direction agrees with plot data, but magnitude differs across WB, STWB, paired and single-catchment methods
Estimate kept despite non-significant residual test (p = 0.78)

end.claim: After 50% strip-thinning, annual STWB water loss in the treated catchment fell from 840 to 780 mm/year. Paired-catchment monthly treatment effects were negative from September 2011 to May 2012 and positive from May to December 2012 (about -20 mm/year net).

decisive_move.sentence: Applying the STWB model to both catchments and then the pre-treatment calibration regression yields the monthly treatment effects; without this estimation there is no seasonal ET claim.

gates.evidence: The thinning treatment and paired monitoring were set up in advance under a broader project (CREST/JSPS). The seasonal-pattern hypothesis is stated only loosely in the introduction (p. 2). The main claim faced a t-test of residuals that it did not pass (p = 0.78, p. 8) and a comparison with plot-scale data (p. 8), yet the claim was kept. No analysis plan or threshold is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Ordinary least-squares linear regression (calibration equation, gap filling)

limits:
No review file was supplied, so only the final-paper sequence is coded.

Internal inconsistencies:
- The abstract lists ET as '840 and 910 and 780 and 860 mm/year in KT and KC, respectively', but Table 3 gives KT 840 to 780 and KC 910 to 860.
- The abstract says ET 'decreased due to 50% thinning were similar or different', which is vague.
- The thinned share is 64% of KT in the Methods but 32% in the Discussion (p. 9).
- The 'pre-thinning' peak water loss is dated 15-25 September 2011, which falls in the operation period (p. 7).

Text extraction: minus signs appear lost in the PDF text, so treatment effects ranged from -30.9 to +20.2 mm/month (inferred from Figure 9).

Uncertainty and testing:
- No uncertainty or resolution is given for the STWB estimates, so the estimate_with_resolution status is generous.
- The residual t-test was non-significant (p = 0.78), yet a treatment effect is interpreted.
- The STWB storage-equality assumption is taken from Suzuki (1985) and not tested here. The groundwater record is shown but not used to check it.

Design scope: only one pre-thinning year and one post-thinning year are used, and the during-operation period is excluded from calibration.

Sub-claim at a different status: understory recovery as the cause of the increased growing-season ET is best_explanation at most. It is supported only by cited understory survey data (Onda & Gomi 2021) and is not tested against the other listed factors.

Independence of the plot-scale check: the comparison data come from Sun et al. (2017), which shares authors (inference: not fully independent).

Other: data are available only on request. The 'contemporary paired catchment analysis on runoff' announced in the Methods (p. 5) has no clearly reported results.

Composition is none_fits: this is a single manipulated paired-catchment experiment estimating an effect, with no rival tested, no repetition and no capability focus.

disagreements.target: Sun et al. (2017) plot-scale ET in catchment KT
disagreements.support: STWB pre-thinning water loss (840 mm) is lower than the plot-scale ET (980 mm), while the post-thinning values match (780 mm).
disagreements.quote: the water loss during the pre-thinning period in the present study was relatively smaller compared to that in Sun et al. (2017)

disagreements.target: Bosch and Hewlett (1982); Stednick (1996) water-yield change per 10% forest-cover change
disagreements.support: The paired-catchment change of about 20 mm/year is far below the 18-50 or about 40 mm per 10% cover change reported in syntheses; precipitation, species and floor evaporation are offered as reasons.
disagreements.quote: Our results showed a much lower water loss changes after 50% strip thinning

disagreements.target: View of thinning as a net water gain
disagreements.support: Monthly treatment effects turn positive about 5 months after thinning, attributed to understory regrowth.
disagreements.quote: The view of thinning as a net water gain may not hold throughout a year if both canopy and understory vegetation regrow rapidly

alternatives_considered.reason: Changes in water storage become apparent at monthly or seasonal scale, so the annual method cannot resolve seasonal ET

alternatives_considered.chosen: Include July 2011 shrub removal in the pre-thinning period
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Treating shrub removal as part of the treatment (implicit)
alternatives_considered.reason: so as to evaluate the effects of overstory vegetation
